BRUNNER, MOND, & CO., LIMITED. The 16th half-yearly ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, was held on Monday, in the Law ,tssnoia- eiation Rooms, Ceok-st.. Liverpool. Mr. John Cros- field, chairman of the board of directors, presided, and there was a large attendance.—ln their report the directors say—. The balance sheet and profit and loss account show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 31st December, 1888, of £102,014 10s. 81., which, with the amount of £20,11.8 13m. Bd. brought forward from the previous half-year, make a total of £122,183 Is. 4d. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follow :—Dividend on the preference capital at 7 per cent. per annum. £11.090 12s. 13d. divi- dend on the ordinary capital at 25 percent per annum, £70,025 ; amount to be written ti patents account, £2,500; amount to he placed to .spense account, £09,000; and balance to he brought forward £17,947 11s. 10d. Thu amount standing to the debit of patents account is now a very inadequate reprmentation of the value of the patents belonging to the company, and the directors, therefore, propose to write off a much smaller amount than hitherto. The reserve fund now stands at a figure which the directors consider mnple for the purpose for which this fund was creatiel, namely, to pmvide for extraordinary emergencies. The dins-tors, however, propose to place to a suspense account the sum of £20,000 towards meeting the cost of a remodelling of a portion of the plant, which they have decided upon to effect economim in the manufacture."—The Chairman thought the shareholders would think tte report a satisfactory one. He moved its adoption, and that the dividends named he paid.—Mr. H. Coghill seconded the motion, which was carried unaninionsly.—£soo was voted to Ihe directors tor their services during the half- vear.—Messrs. John Creslield, Edward Milner, and 11. Coghill were re-elected directors, and Mr. T. W. Read was re-appointed auditor. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.

The fifty-fourth sitting of the Parnell Commission, on Thursday, will be a memorable one. The court was crowded, the next intense interest was shown in the proceedings, and the statements of Mr. Pigott with regard to the interview with Mr. Labouchere, and more particularly under the searching crom-esamiration by Sir Charles Russell, were not sorely sensational, but altogether novel, and at times almost dramatic. ('on- tinning his evidence on tie resumption of the inquiry, Mr. Pigott spoke of his visits to Lausanne and his pew • ,alo to Davis, who agreed to write apaniphlet for £lOO f such a task was not likely "to interfere with the relations between the Fenian Brotherhood and Mr. Par- nt•ll." The witness then dealt with kit visit to Paris in 1886, when he meta man who styled himself Maurice Murphy and said he was an agent of the Clan-na-Gael, but did not know anything of the important documents Davis had rnentioned. At an mterview a few days later, however, Murphy said he had actually discovered the bag con- taining the documents—letters from Mr. Parnell and Egan. Mr. Pigott told Murphy that he was authorised to buy such documonts, and Murphy first asked £l,OOO and then £5OO for the contents of the hag The tug was then produced. There were five letters—int-Wing the lac-sunlit—alleged to have been written by Mr. Parnell and in said to be written by Egan. Then he detailed his conference with Mr. Houston, las journey to New York, where be obtained the waled letter from Breslin authorising the transfer of the precious documents, his return to harm, and Mr. Houston's visit to that city, and the purchase from Murphy of the letters for £5OO, the witness himself receiving 100 guineas commission. Murphy some weeks afterwards sought to get the letters back, but did not succeed. The story as to how he obtained the other batches of letters from •• Tom Brown." and another person unknown, caused some mirth ; and his extraordinary interview with Mr. Labouchere, Mr. Parnell, and Mr. George Lewis also entertained the court. The death occurred on Saturday, under the moot distressing circumstances, of Mr. J. B. Yeomans who lived at IS, Lovely-lane, and who was well. and much respected in the town. 111-health made its appearance in the family of Mr. Yeomans at the commencement of the year, when Mrs. Yeo- mans was confined to had suffering from an attack of some inflammatory disease of the lungs. One of the children, seven years of age, died from scarlet fever on the .2.2nd of Jannary, and on the tith of the same month a second Child of Mr. Yeomans, Prank, aged three, was admitted to the Infectious Diseases Hospital. suffering from the name malady, to which he succumbed on the first day of the present month. On the tegli of January, a third child from the same family, a girl of live years of age, was admitted into the hospital and is DOW, fortunately, progressing favourably. The infection was afterwards caught by the father, who was taken ill, and died at his residence on Saturday morning. Universal and deep sympathy has been expressed for the bereaved I widow and mother, wits has in so short a time lost her husband and two children. There are two children yet living to comfort her. The late Mr. mmans, who was one of the Churchwardens of the 1 parish of St. Barnabas, was :13 years of age, and was employed at the offices of Messrs. Pearson and 1 Knowles' Coal and Iron Company, Bewsey-road. , He was at one time known as a prominent and stmcessf ul athlete, and frequently officiated as han- dicapper at local athletic meetings. The remains of the deceased were interred at the Cemetery on Monday afternoon.

Before Mr. John Brundrat and Dr. Steele, at Runcorn l'etty Sessions on Monday,Daniel Williams, landlord of the Cornwall and Devonshire Inn IChurch-st., Was summoned for having on the DA inst., been drunk on his own licensed premises.-. P.C. Hulse stated that about half-past four on the I day in question he saw a crowd about the Inn, awl ; on going there he found that toe door was smashed. i Ile went inside and saw the defendant there its a very intoxicated condition and quarrelling with hie mother-in-law.- -P.C. Carrington said the defendant was drunk and unfit to have charge of the house. Mr. F. A. Lake defended, and stated that on this day the defendant was suffering from neuralgia and while show- , ink a friend from Swansea, the docks, Runcorn Bridge , and the other sitian oof the town, he was persuaded to Like sixpennyworth of "rum " to ease the pain. On arriving forme at four o'clock, Inc found his I dinner w-as not ready and sullorring front the irri- tation consequent upon the tomthache he began to "blow up hiA wife for her neglect. Ilia wife naturally retorted that if he wanted his dinner he must come harm at a proper hour. They got to hot I words, and the mother-in-law took the wife's part. Dur- ing the squabble,the mother-in-law was leavingtbe house and the defendant was preventing her, when the door was sharply closed, r rid the glass -vlnicln was cracked was smashed, and fell into the street, calming a com- motion amongst the children just mnming from school. Mr. Like submitted that when the officers entered the house, tine defend:tic was not suffering from an undue quantity of drink, but from an overdose of mother-in-- law, (laughter) and instead of beMg draggisl there, lie was deserving of the sympathy or: the officers.—The defendant was sworn and corroboratmi this statement, denying that he was drunk.—The wife and mother-in- law gave similar evidence.—Mr. Brundrit said in the excitement of the moment the defendant tnight have appeared to be drunk, and as there was In doubt in the ease, the defendant would have the benefit, and he was discharged.

The fourth session of the twelfth Parliament of Queen Victoria was opened by Royal Commission. There was an unusually large number of ladies on the peers' lynches, on the floor of the House, and in the strangers' gallery, but the attendance of peers was small. At two o'clock the Lord Chancellor, preceded by the inactsbeirer and purse-hearer, entered the House and fonnally took his seat I m the woolsack. The Colter of the Black Rod summoned the Speaker and members of the House of Commons to hear the Commission and the ,1 Queen's Speech read, and Mr. Speaker, accompanied by I the Sergeant-at-Anon and many members of the House of Commons, attended at the bar. Mr. Bethel read the I Commission, and _
The LORD Cledneln.l.oll then. "at Her Majewty's command," read the Queen's speech as follows THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. -- •

Mr LORDS AND GINNTLEMIN.—During the Brief period that has elajned sines the close of the not session nothing has taken place to affect the cordial relations which exist between myself and other Powers. The operations which had been successfully completed in Egypt a few days before the last prorogation have effected the object for which they were undertaken, and I see no ground for apprehending the renewal of disturbanee in the neighbourhood ef Suakin]. The negotiations which 1 dineted to be opened with the rulers of 'Millet for the purpose of preventing encroachment on my rights over the territory of Sikkim have not 4. yet been brought to a favourable ronclusion, but I hope that further military operations will not he 1.011,117. I have consented to take part in a conference with Germany and the United States at Berlin upon the affairs of Samoa, in continuation of that which wan recently : assembled at Washington.

Giorrraistere oc en.. House or Comuoss,--The esti- mates for the public service of the year will be laid before ' you. The unceasing expenditure upon warlike prepare- ! tion which has been incurred by other European nations ! ' has rendered necessary an increase in the premutions which have hitherto 'been taken for the safety of our !shores and our commerce. The counsels by smolt other Powers are guided, and which dispose of their vast : forces, aro at present uniformly friendly to this country, but I have no right to assume that this condition is necessarily secure from the poesibility of change. MT LORDS AND GANTLIOTNN,—Some portions of the. bill which was presented to you not year for amending I ! the local government of England and Wales were laid I aside in consequence of the pressure upon the time of Parliament, and from the same cause it was found to be impossible to enter upon the imention of local govern- ment for Scotland. Hills dealing with these matters will be laid before you. Your early attention will be asked to measures for developing the material resources of iridand, and for amending, the constitution of the various tribunals which have special jurisdiction over teal property in that country. The statutes which you have recently passed for the restoration of order and e-onfidence in Ireland have already been attended with salutary results. Legislative provision will he necessary fee executing the convention into which I have entered for the sup- ! :17:err iof tiTet'intgi'th'emeolihi7eraiMn rottnYat vague, and I Annuities.
The state of the gold coinage has for some year.s imst been the suhiect of legitimate complaint. A /11PASUIV for restoring it to a satisfactory condition will he laid before you:. . . . _ . . . .

Though the commission whirh I appointed to inquirer into the civil eatablishments of the United Kingdom has not yet completGl its labours, it haa already made a report of much value, and projr.ds for legislation arising out of that report will be submitted to you. Several subjects which I have commended to your ears in previous years, but which the increa-sing burden IA ' your dltties has shut out from consideration, will be sub- mitted to you again. Ire this number will be included ineaduns relating to tithes, for the regulation of the Universities of Scotland, or determining the liabilities of employers in the ease of accidents, for establishing a Department of Agricugure, for cheapening the Ganef, of land, and for remodying abuses attaching to joint- stock coninaniffs formed under limited liability. I pray that the Missing of Almighty tied may he with you in the diachargu of your arduous duties. div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

After being stopped tar about.. fortnight, the steam pile driver has this week again con 1111 l owed operations. Upwards of 20 large wooden piles have been driven into ! the sand tank opposite the old ferry, and as the nwhine works with great ease and expediiion this number may be quickly doubled. At the West side of Runcorn Bridge the concrete wall is being rapidly construetcsl. There is now about 300 feet of wall ready for coping, and a large gang of men is engaged in constructing • further length of wain a copper dam about 80 feet long. The work is being carried on night and day. Mr. tiregson, the agent, is on the spot at all hours, and so that he can more conveniently carry out his onerous duti,t, he has had a comfortable sittinfproom fitted up on the works. At Norton the construction of the Randall sluices is pro- ceeding apace, and they are now in a forward state. NEAR W'ARRINGTON. . . . . . . . . . .

The neighbourhoisl id' the intended Latchforillks it one of the busiest parts of the canal at present. There are ' here about half-a-dozen steam navvies regularly at work , and on both sides of the cutting rapid progress is Is Mg made with the huge embankments for the deviated line of the Warrington and Altrineham railway. A number ! of workmen areal. engaged in preparing tha founda- tion for the embankment near Latchford station. Many workmen are continuously employed on the route of the ianal near the upper parts of Wash-lane, Latchford, and , between there and Stockton Heath. 1 THE CANAL AND THE WARRINGTON WATER SUPPLY.

The Warrington Water Works Company's water will be carried lw two subways under the Ship Canal near St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath. The whole sup- ply of the Winwick water will pass thivaigh the nab-war round the Mulberry Tree, per a large new main which is to be SCon lying by the rivatiside. A new main will run underneath" the highway by Lumbrook bridge ; thence along Ackers.lane to Grappenhall.road, near Mr. Wal- lington', house, where it will terminate for the present ; hut it is probable that eventually it may be extended to I irappenhall, Thelwall, be. Another main will be laid from Stockton Heath Vicarage along the new road to Walton Pool, on the Chester.road, in the direction of : Moore, which is alreatly supplied with water. About 100 I.;,;Zpli7y7sl—;;—the .11;1;a11 section of the Ship Canal, near Warrington, abandoned their work on Monday inconsequence ol their being refused an increase in wages. Their are paid at the rare of 24d. per hour, but, they demanded an increase of 4-‘l. per hour, which was ref usod, and they thereupon left their work, and created a disturbance on the railway by placing obstacles in front oft lie locomotives, and turning the points, men having to he appointed to fill their places. Most of the boys have, however, since wormed to work, but the ringleaders, who numbered a dozen, were dis- charged.

div.head: taDNES LOCAL BOARD AND THE CANAL.
div.p: taDNES LOCAL BOARD AND THE CANAL.

At a special meeting of the Widnes Local Board, held yesterday afternoon, the Chairman reported that Mr. Carey, Mr. Liddell and himself, and a deputation from ! the Traders Association, consisting of Major Cross and Mr It Wade Deacon, had an interview with Mr. Leader Williams, engineer to the Ship Canal, with regard to tho proposed deviation (routine plans in tho construction of the sluices and the rising of water in the canal 10 ! inches. Mr. Leader Williams argued that these altem- Dons would be to the advantage of Widnes. To pour through the sluices at low water a vast volume of water would scour the river more effectively ! than a constant overflow at all states of the tide. He aLso pointed out that the lock which it had been intended to construct apposite to the Belvedere at Runcorn would be constructed near the Old Quay, and that DID would al.) be an improvement. He further infonned the deputation that it was intended to make a large dock on land they mod obtained an ',mistime Marsh, at the mouth of the river Weaver ; and stated it would be to the advantage of Widnes to send their carges for America and other places to that dock and load them into the steamers there than to send it down to Liverpool. The deputation desired that an engineer should be consulted as to the effect the alterations in the canal and sluices would have upon the estuary ; and on the proposition of Mr. Ifeyes,seconded by Mr. Taylor, it was resolved that an engin..., should he consulted accordingly.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN,
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN,

That the meeting held at Widnes to denounce the imprisonment and treatment of Mr. William O'Brien woo a most enthusiastic gathering, and the comprehensive and strongly worded resolution was carried without a dissentient vote.

That there are no hopes entertained that Mr. MOS. Will "recommend " the resolution to the Howie of Commons, and the home Rulers are impatiently waiting fora General Election in order to once more attempt to retrieve the mistake made in 18S5, wh-n Mr. Misspratt was rejected. That Mr. Muspratt received a very flattering ovation on his first public appearance since his elevation to the Ablermanic Bench of the Celerity Council, and regret was expressed that Mr. Simi* was not present to inspire the audience with his earnest eloquence and inexhaustible fund of appro- priate anecdote. That a meeting of the members of the Council of the Liberal Association in Runcorn North was held on Tuesday evening. Mr. W. Ockleston, chainnan of the district, was present, and received a most cordial welcome, the members recognising with gratification that lie evidently intended to he, not a kid glove politician, but a real hardworking, aggressive leader of the party ill the town. He gave a satisfactory explanatien of the circtinastance that led him to decline the invitation of the party to contest Runcorn North at the recent County Council election, and hinted that at some future , time,if they desired, his services should be willingly !placed at their disposal. ' That Mr. Ockleston introduced the question of establishing a Liberal Club, and there was a unanimous acquiescence in his views that it was a necessity and would be of the greatest possible advantage to the party. Practical instructions were given to Mr. R. Moore, the district secretory, and a committee was appointed to obtain inform- ation and take steps for achieving the end in view. From what can be heard and seen "then' is every probability that club will be successfully formed in the course of a brief period, and the reflection cast urn the sturdy Liberalism of Runcorn by the clubs in other parts of the Division will be swept

That Mr. Brunner is expected to he present at the annual meeting of the Liberal COIIIICII of the Divi- sion, to be held at Northwich to-day. That the figures given at the meeting of the ('o-operative Society on Wednesday suggests an idea. In moat of the societies in Lancashire a certain proportion of the benefits is set aside for educational purposes, and in ninny instances splen- did libraries and newsrooms, are maintained. Run- corn Society out of its great profit of nearly £ll,OOO last year contributed not a penny to such a purpose. If tl.e Committee were to contribute .C 10. a year to the Runcorn and Widnes Free Libraries, there would be no appreciable diminution in the dividend and two deserving institutions would receive much needed aid.

That the. majority of the members would not object to such a donation, if the subject were properly placed before them. That an unusual scene occurred on the platform at Runcorn station at midnight on Wednesday. Mr. Allan Cunningham, son of the late respected Mr. W. G. Cunningham. was departing for London by the expreas to route for Australia in search of the Fame and fortune which is en difficult of attainment . in the mother country, and about tal of his friends and acquaintances gathered to wish him (tad speed. There were many friendly exchanges,and much hand '1 shaking, and the strains of "Auld Lang Sync" I awoke the silence of the night. As the train moved from the platform an encouraging shout burst from every throat to encourage the wanderer on his way. Mr. Cunningham was accompanied by Mr. Frank Pierce,a friend from Eccles, who lam relativm : iu Sydney.

Whatever of romance or sentiment used to be attached to the vocation of the hand.on weaver, there CAR be no doubt that most of it was stamped out with the advent of steam and the factory system. Curzon, /111.1`., who contributed to the Fm.t.,i•rhtly Perim of January an admirable article on "A visit In Itokhare— once the Athens of Central Asia,—thus describes the women of this ancient city have frequently been asked situ, my return—it is a question which an Eng- lishman always seems south first—whet the women of ' Itoklitira were like? I am utterly unable to say. I never saw the features of one between the ages of ten and fifty. The little girls ran about, unveiled, in loose silk frocks, and wore their hair in long plaits escaping from a tiny skull cap. Si 11l flatly the old hags were allowed to exhibt their innocuous charms on the ground, I sup- pose, that they could excite no dangerous emotions. But the hulk of the female population were veiled in a man- tra. that defied and even repelled scrutiny. For not only were the features concealed behind a heavy black horsehair veil, falling from the top of the head to the bosom; but their figures were loosely wrapped up in ' big blue cotton dressing gowns, the sleeves of which are not lIAPIi but are pinned together over the shoulders 00 11,,' back and hang down to the ground, where from under this shapeless 112.1911 of drapery appear a pair of feet encased in bit leather boots. Orr.—l am not going to suggest means tor curing Colds in this paper; I do enough, I hunk, for one day, ill indicate plans or methods of prevention. And I cannot surely better effect my object than by trying to explain when applied cold is danger- ous, and when it is merely a bugbear. I have given one example in my own person; the corollary is—beware of draughts. There is danger. I mean, in having one pot, lion of the holy exposed to chill, the other portions being wane. Example s—l do maintain and defy con- tradiction in saying that many thousands of people owe their fatal illnesses to colds caught in bed. For here the front of the chest is kept warm, as are the arms and whole body—the face and head excepted, but they are inured—while the one wee morsel left exposed to chill, especially in those who sleep on the side, is not much bigger. perhaps, than the heel of Achilles, and lies be. 0.111 the naps of the neck and between the shoulder Hades. Hove you never felt cold just there. reader, towards morning of a winter night? Prob-ct that spot. lldelicate,. there where the cheat should be shielded by a cheat protector. People subject to colds in the chest should do all they can—and that is a god deal—to pre- vent recurrence of their complaints. We hear people say sometimes, " Yes, I ain rather subject to colds, but they dou't last long." Many and teamed have been the debates as to whether St. Oswald fell at Winwick,or Oswestry, or in Northumberland. oswahl was the champion of Christianity, and he was opimsed by l'enda, whose 11l e was one long battle against the Cross. lie was the enlightened king of Northumbria. On one oec:ision. when sitting down to a feast, he beard hat at his gate there were a number of poor who wanted sustenance, and he ordered the silver dishes ire be lnk,noeet untested and divided among them. May ties hand never grow old," said Bishop Aidan when he seized the Kings hand and blessed it; and according to the legends of the time, when Oswald was defeated and slain by l'enda in 619 and the savage conqueror mutilated him, the "white hand which Aldan had blessed remained without blemish. But much more recent events make Winwick interesting. During the Civil War the Duke of Hamilton entered England with 17.000 men, and Sir Marmaduke Langdale marched south from Northumberland with a large force. Cromwell met them, and, falling on Sir Marmaduke's division, he quite routed it, and cut off all communication with the Scots. list the lkike's army was still intact, and they retreated to Winwick, when a sanguinary battle was fought, the site of which is still pointed out. Cromwell, as usual, was vP;torious.

At Winwiek there is a free grammar school, founded hy Canner Legit in 160 U, and here Richard Alather was a scholar, lie went after- wards to Liverpool to take charge of a public school, and subsequently took Ins degree at Brasenoee College and entered the Church. But the worldli- ness he saw in the ambitions and preferments of ecclesiastics induced him to resign ltis living, and ho was one of the early settlers in Massachusetts. llis youngest son was Increase .lather, and his grandson was the celebrated Cotton Mather, whose descendanto are among the foremost people in the

WIN WICK. (Prom the' Manchester Guardian.") Winwick lies between three and four miles from Warrington, on the road to Newton-in-the-Willows, and it is one of the most delightful spots in this part of England. The road from Warrington is very pleasant, awl it increases in interest as we , pass by the grounds and shrubberies attached. to Winwick Hall. These are celebrated for their rhododendrons, which are hardly surpassed anf - I where for splendour. They are of very old growt It is said they most closely resemble those growing by the Black Km, whence they originally came. The living of. Winwick, it is scarcely necessary to say, is one of the most valuable in England; in Lancashire, and Doddington, in Cambridgeshire, being Irocketed in the same privileged categor,Y. According to the last returns, the living of in Lancashire, is isot down at ed,501) a year, W in- wick at .E.3:2111), and Doddington ( which has a population ol 1,;55. Dissenters included) at the more modest 811111 of /1,700. But the charm of Winwick lies in its Met must]oe situation, ahnost uninvaded by modem improvements. Round the church are some very noble yews. The spire I. tisible from more than on, railway, aud its solid

div.head: lUSE E,
div.p: lUSE E,

New World. While in Liverpool. it is said, the great and self-taught astronomer Jeremiah Bor. rocks was his pupil. In Winwick Church is a monument to Mrs. Legit of Lyme, who died soon after her marriage, and whose history is romance itself. She was the heiress of Shrigley Hall and the large estates that belonged to it. At the age of fifteen pile was at a boarding school in Liverpool, and of course was looked upon as a prize. There was a Miss Francea Wakefield, who was the daughter of Dr. Davis, the head master of Macclesfield Grammar School, who had two nephews, Edward Gibbon Wakefield and William Wakefield and she hit upon a plan to abduct the heiress for her nephew Edward Gibbon. They went in a carriage to the school in Liverpool where Miss Turner was, and hy false pretences I hey induced her to go to Gretna Green, where the historic black- smith married the young people,for,as he said," two a gnineas nd champagne.. ' They escaped with their prize to France, hut the lady was rescued by her uncle in Calais. The Wakefield, were alterwards tried at Lancaster, and sentenced to three years' imprisonment. Mr. Legh, of Lyme was tire magis- trate before whom they were first brought, and he afterwards married the young lady. She died at the age of nineteen, and s sculptured monument is erected toiler in Winwiek Church. There are many other monuments of interest in the church, which is in a district of exceptional beauty ; and whether we approach it from Newton. or Earlestown, Or Warrington the walk is a delightful one.

An the sun slowly rank behind the high create of the Western Sierras' throwing long linon of yellow light which seemed to quiver in the air of the arm., and cast shadows which looked like strangely distorted silhouettes, Ohl Dandy went shunting along, hie ragged clothes, brokemout boots, bleared eyes and rut face i-howing only too plainly hie claim to being considered—on he wee, en fact, generally conaidered—a hopelessly irre- claimable drunkard. Ilia furtive look at this man or that, as he plesed them—ri look which would have been appealing were it not for the "bleari- ness "of the eyes from which it came—gave only too plain evidence that a lung course of whisky had cowed the man'o spirit oompletely ; had reduced him to a worse connition than that of a dog. Old Dandy's shaking hand could scarcely lift a glass of the fiery liquor that was ruining him to his lips, and there was onto man in camp that could not bully him as much as he liked. It had not alwaye been so. Twenty years Wore, when Henry Preston came to the mines first, he won a man that few would care to provoke. Hard work, and plenty of it, had made him a good miner, and his shrewdness reeulted—ae shrewdness and hard work always will—in the rapid accumulation of money, lJnfortunately for hire, drinking took hold of him, and as the years went by he gradually lost property, money and standing, sinking lower and lower, until he became "Old Dandy." His name was forgotten, even by himself, seemingly, and that given to him in mockery of his rags was the only one by which he wale known. It seemed as though he had but one friend in the camp, and he was a man who, of all that motley throng, would probably have been the last one who would have been picked out as the " pard " of the drunken loafer. For Jack Holloway was ono of the few men in camp who never drank at all. Full of life and spirits—one of the beet and most efficient workers there—he was always ready for any kindof fun, although he would not drink and he would not gamble. Them peculiarities would, under ordinary circumstances, have rendered him highly unpopular, but no one could resist the charm of Jack's manner, and it wee sufficient that a man was in trouble for Jack to come to his aid. It mud have been this that made Jack Old Dandy's only friend, for certainly it could be nothing el.. In Jack's cabin there won always something to eat, and thither Dandy was making his way that hot July evening in search of a meal.
" Hello, ol man !" said Jack, an the door opened and Dandy sidled into the cabin. " Come for grub Well, it's post ready. Sit down." . _
" Thank 'ee, Jack; thank 'cc," was the humble answer, as Dandy sat down on one of the candle boxes which served as seats.
The two men ate in alienee, only broken by Jack's remark
--•-•-fak;;Onto. coffee. Dandy. It'll to you
At the end of the meal Jack filled hi pipe, sod, pushing the tobacco over to hie guest, looked at him narrowly. drinkin' today, Dandy l" "No Jack. New a drink."

“Look here, el man. I've been thinkin"bont you lately, au' 11l gin' you show. I'm gobs' out promectin' to-morrow, an' if you'll go I'll furnish the grub stake, providlie you'll transfer your share of anything we get to me, to hold in trust for you. I sint goin to hey you putting up your share agin licher. What do you eay ” "I'd like to do it, Jack; like it mighty well. I /epos° you wouldn't take a little whisky with you, case we got hurt." "Not a drop," said Jack, resolutely. "I know you, Dandy. I know if I get the licker out of you you're as good a prospector as thur is going. That'. why I'll go shares. But I aint going to take you off to the hills to get you drunk, not if I know myself. Now, will you do it; Be • moo, Dandy. Brace up, and show you've got something in you." "I'm afraid it's too late, Jack." Nonsenee, ol' man. 'Taint toyer too late to pu'l'lldoYit7Jsat k'un:strlml illlyoduonttrioNganh.d" for ths first time in months Dandy seemed to really straighten himself up. The next day. Jack having provided Dandy with • snit of brown jeans, a pair of shoes and some blankets, the strangely asoorted couple mounted and rode off. Striking to the north they prospected carefully, camping a night. Dandy improved wonderfully. 'The pure mountain air, the hard work, and the regularity in the matter of meal., brought him back to eomething like his old form, and as the days Hew swiftly by, he began to once more feel and act like a man. fie did good work, two, It was Dandy whose knowledge of mining and great erperionce enabled the two to trace the float rock which finally led them to the location of the famous " Star of the North." It was Dandy's careful examination wick really revealed the extra. ordinary richness of that great mining property, Jack, when he picked Dandy out for a partner, showed good judgment, and although he did much for the old man, the result proved that he had done as much for himself.

As they were riding down the trail, on their way to the camp, Jack .gave Dandy a good talking to on the aubject of drinking, and the reply, I aint going to get inter that or bog agin, Jack," gave him some confidence in the cure. For all that, the first thing he did was to take Dandy to the office of the mining recorder, and get the deed of trust signed. Jack was wine in his generation, and took no ehmees.

The news of the discovery and /creation of the "Star of the North," and the ..ight of the apeci• mona, produced a decided sensation. Dandy Omen more became a man of conererm mce in the corn. triunity, and many men were anxioua to show their liking for him by standing drinks. But the old men was firm.

" obleeged to you, Cy," he said, some day, to Cy Hawkins, when the latter suggested a "whisky sour," "but my pardner an' me hea agreed thar's no drinkin' to be done by the firm, I guess I'll wait till he begins." Cy reported the answer, and the amazement of the camp at Handy's reformation was almost swallowed up in their amusement at the idea sag. gated by him of Jack's taking a drink. The "Star of the North" speedily found capital to develop it, and the two partners found themselves with money. Jack regularly gave Dandy his allowance, and a radical change in the appearance of the old man was the result. He became quite respectable, as far as clothes went. He did not do much work about the mine: but his advice was of enormous value to Jack, who had been appointed superintendent. One afternoon, whoa Jack was at the post-office, Higgins, the local representative of the government, naked him if he knew any man by the name of Henry Preston. Jack thought for a moment and then suddenly exclahuml "Why of course, thata Dandy." "Wan!," rejoined Higgins, " thar 'e a letter for him here as hez bin here fur a week. You'd better take it. Wonder who 's awritiu' to the old man ?"
—fhe receipt of this letter threw Dandy into a kind of brown study for the next two days. Finally he unburdened hilosell to JaLk.
said he, "1 guebo I 'II bey to go down to the Bay."
-s; What' for ?" demanded Jack, shortly. s.Wa'al, the fact I. I've got a little girl=
6.1 left the States when my wife net the baby I left with my sister, It Lel:3llM nhe 's coniing out here; fact is, she 'a come au I must go. meet beg."
--;; Well. I'm bleseed. What on eurth are you goin' to do with her here?" " dune°, Jack, but it 'pears to me I'll hey' to go fur her." "I 'spore so. Look here, Dandy, don't you drink down here."

"I ain't. gobs' to Jack. I've had enough of it. Don't you be afraid to, that." The next day Dandy started I) y the sta,'e. His errand could not be kept a secret, aml during his absence the camp got into the wiliest state of excitement over" Dandy's gal," as she was Speculation as to her appearanee and age were rife, and the moat absurd theories were broached upon the aubjeet. The general belief seemed to be that she woo very large. Dandy hin.elf wax stall man, with black hair and a somewhat ahrewdish disposition; and Jack was freely commiserated with upon the fact that he would he obliged to one more or less of her.

"Jerk, " said —Cy Hawkins', "that ar gal o' Daody's in &nein ter make you an' th' ol' man stand around now. You hear me squeal ; " and Cy wan felt by the crowd to have expressed the opinion of the majority. . . .
, Jack himself looked upon tho addition to the society in the cabin with anything but favour.
Atte'r an &bunco of about ten days, when the eoaeh drew up at the door of Suiuzins'e.

said Dandy, "tm,, yid Illy daughter, Gerty. Gerty, tho' s the bryn." The boys bowed awkwardly enough, and be came unplerantly eonseions id the patches which decorated m arabesques their various garments. Miss (icily bowed, and turning to her father, said :
--"Father, I would like to wash my hands and face ; there was so much dust on the road." Three of the boys promptly reeled off, calling, "Major," at the top of their voice,. „ . . .

Major fmuggrns appearing, a room was se cured, into which Miss I:erty was shown. When rho disappeared evcry man in the crowd shook hands with Henry, come of thorn two or three times. But all D coly wantr.l to know was about Jack. He had writs, u that he was corn. log, but the letter had not arrived ; no Jack WM not there. Major Suiggins offered his waggon to take Dandy and Miss truly to the mine, twelve miles away; aud the oiler being accepted, the three drove otf, much to the disgust of " the boys." When the party arrived at the mire, Jack Wafl seated in front of the raisin, occupied ,42 the useful work of putting a patch, out from a flour sack, into the knee of a pair of trousers. When he saw the waggon drive up he hastily put the things away, and stood there blushing to the roots of his hair as Dandy sad the girl jumped out. Gerty," said the old man, "this is Jack."

7 "1 know Jack very well, ' was the amiling on- .won " Do you know that although my father hoe done nothing but talk about you I do not know your loot name? " "foe Jack Holloway," said the owner of the last name, confusedly. 4.1 am afraid that your father has talked too much about me."
"Nary time, Gerty ; don'tiou believe him. He's the best man you ever see." " Nonsense, Dandy!" said Jack, more c.nnfused than ever.
Miss Gerty broke in "1. this where you lire, tether?" "Ye,. Won't you come inside?"

The two wet into the cabin, which, though large, was in the state of indescrible confusion which generally characterizes any place run by men alone, Jack cloud outside and glanced at Sniggins, who winked. The wink /teemed to com- plate the discomfiture of the young superintendent. He turned away, and just then Dandy and his daughter came out, and the major drove off. It was speedily settled that the two men were to sleep in the office of the works until they could build an addition to the cabin. In • few days this was done, and the three lived tranquilly together. A wandering Chinese was captured for a cook. Miss Gerty took charge of the house, and the men lived more comfortably than they had for a long time. Having money, Jack by degrees became something of a swell, as far as clothes went. He got a horse for Miss Gerty to ride, and took CO riding with her. The girl seemed to like him very well, and, as far as he was concerned, he was evidently very much in love with her. Months slipped away in this manner, and although there did not seem to be much change in affairs, it was • matter of some surprise to the men in the camp that Jack had not fixed things before. The fact of the matter was that Jack, while as bold as a gristly ordinarily, was, as far as Gerty was con- cerned, in a state of abject terror. A dozen times he had made up his mind to speak, and a dozen times he had hared to put his late to the test Onc day Jack was walking along the path from the mill to the cabin when he heard Gerty's voice up a little ravine, crying for help. To dash up to the spot and to seize the man with whom she was struggling, and throw him down • ith such force as to leave him imeneible, was for Jack not much more than a moment's work. The man turned out to be one of the mill hands, rather drunk, who had been trying to snatch a kiss. As Jack stood there, with his arm around the girl who was clinging to him, his fear vaniahed, and he said
darling, you are not hurt l" " No, Jack ;' aud as tie.rty clung closer to hint Jack knew it was all right. lie beat down and bitted her..

" Don't hurt him any were. Jack," murmured the girl, "for my sake." " Very well, dear." The two left the place and walked hand in hand to the cabin. Entering it, Jack said to Dandy "Old man, I love Getty, and she loves me. Will you give her to me ?" Dandy glanced at Geriye blushing face for a moment, and then said "Gladly, Jack. No one in the world else." And then Gerty ran away into her own room, and the two men shook hands. ..."

That afternoon, when Jack was at the mill, Dandy called Gerty ous to him on the porch. " My little girl," he said, stroking her hair as she sat on • stool beside him, "you kin never know what Jack did for me. I were • common drunkard 'round this camp, despised by all, sold body and BOW to liquor. J ack usca to give me my grub and • place to sleep. Ile woo' the only friend I had, One day he said to me if I'd go prospectin' with him he'd giv' me • chance. I was 'feared, but Jack stuck to me, an' now I'm a man ag'in. He's the best man in the world, en' you've got the best husband."
As the old man stopped, Jack's step wan heara coming around the corner. Gcrty got up, and aa Jack put his arm around her and kissed her, Dandy said:
I've told Gerty how you pulled me out of tho hole I wee in."
"I love you more than ever, dear," whispered the girl. "There weent no 'casion to tell her, Dandy, but the count's on my side now. No man over got seal a fee for a cure before.
